description: Astroglia es un equipo interdisciplinario apasionado por la exploración espacial, la salud humana y la tecnología. Buscamos desarrollar soluciones de software innovadoras para monitorear la salud de los astronautas durante misiones espaciales. Invitamos a personas creativas con habilidades en medicina, programación, IA, análisis de datos, ingeniería, diseño UX/UI e investigación científica. Si te apasiona la ciencia, el trabajo en equipo y resolver desafíos reales.
summary:
HANAN PACHA — Integrated Astronaut Health Monitoring Platform
Astronauts face unique physical and psychological challenges during space missions, particularly due to microgravity, confinement, and radiation exposure. With limited access to immediate medical assistance, monitoring their health becomes essential.
To address this challenge, we developed HANAN PACHA, a digital platform that brings different aspects of astronaut health together in one place.
Our platform combines cardiovascular, respiratory, and metabolic monitoring with physical fitness, sleep, cognitive performance, psychological well-being, and radiation exposure tracking. It is designed to integrate data from ECG, Holter monitors, ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, pulse oximetry, and EEG. We also incorporate the three-minute Brief Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT-B) to assess attention and reaction time, alongside the Mental Health Checklist (MHCL) to support psychological monitoring.
Through automated data analysis, HANAN PACHA helps visualize health trends, identify meaningful changes, and support informed medical decisions over time.
We believe protecting astronauts is just as important as developing the technology that takes them into space. With HANAN PACHA, we hope to support safer missions, better health monitoring, and greater medical autonomy as humanity explores beyond Earth.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

HANAN PACHA is an integrated human health monitoring platform designed to address the biomedical challenges of space missions, particularly long-duration exploration missions. Its primary objective is to consolidate physiological, cardiovascular, respiratory, metabolic, muscular, cognitive, psychological, and radiation exposure data into a centralized digital environment, enabling individualized and longitudinal health monitoring for each astronaut.

The proposed system is structured around six complementary modules:

1. Metabolic and respiratory monitoring. A metabolic mask is designed to analyze respiratory gas exchange by measuring oxygen consumption (VO₂) and carbon dioxide production (VCO₂). These parameters provide information about energy metabolism, ventilation, and physiological responses to exercise. They can also support aerobic capacity assessment through appropriate testing protocols.

2. Cardiovascular and respiratory monitoring. The system incorporates a biomedical vest equipped with electrocardiographic (ECG) sensors to record cardiac electrical activity and measure heart rate. Respiratory rate monitoring is also contemplated through compatible sensors. This module aims to track cardiovascular adaptations, heart rate variations, and cardiorespiratory responses during rest, exercise, and recovery.

3. Blood oxygenation monitoring. A pulse oximeter measures peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO₂) and pulse rate, providing complementary information about the astronaut's oxygenation status.

4. Radiation exposure monitoring. A personal dosimeter records individual exposure to ionizing radiation and estimates cumulative radiation dose throughout the mission. This information is organized within a dedicated platform module, allowing individual radiation exposure to be tracked over time.

5.Sleep, cognitive performance, and mental health monitoring. A digital assessment module incorporates periodic sleep monitoring, psychomotor vigilance assessments such as the Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT-B), and psychological assessment tools such as the Mental Health Checklist (MHCL). These tools help evaluate sustained attention, reaction time, and different dimensions of psychological well-being. Their results are recorded to identify changes throughout the mission.

Data from these modules are organized within a centralized digital platform that allows users to visualize health indicators, access individual records, and compare measurements over time. HANAN PACHA therefore aims to transform individual biomedical measurements into integrated health information that supports astronaut health surveillance.

2. What are its benefits?

One of the biggest challenges in space medicine is understanding how different systems of the human body respond to spaceflight, especially during long-duration missions. Microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, confinement, and disrupted sleep patterns can affect astronauts in different ways, from cardiovascular function and muscle health to cognitive performance and psychological well-being.

Monitoring these changes often involves several medical devices and assessment tools, each producing its own information. With HANAN PACHA, we want to bring these different measurements together in one platform, making it easier to understand each astronaut's health as a whole rather than looking at individual results separately.

Our main goal is to turn biomedical measurements into useful information that can be followed throughout a mission. By organizing health records over time, the platform can help identify changes, recognize trends, and support medical assessments when needed.

1. Cardiovascular monitoring and adaptation to microgravity

The proposed biometric vest incorporates electrocardiographic (ECG) sensors to monitor cardiac electrical activity and heart rate. When the ECG signal is of sufficient quality, it may also be possible to analyze heart rate variability (HRV), including measurements such as RMSSD, to better understand changes in autonomic regulation.

This is particularly important because microgravity affects how fluids are distributed throughout the body and can lead to cardiovascular adaptations. Some of these changes may also contribute to difficulties maintaining blood pressure when astronauts return to Earth's gravity.

By following cardiovascular measurements over time, HANAN PACHA could help identify patterns that deserve closer medical attention.

2. Respiratory and metabolic monitoring

HANAN PACHA also proposes integrating a metabolic mask and a pulse oximeter to provide information about respiratory function and energy metabolism.

The metabolic mask measures oxygen consumption (VO₂) and carbon dioxide production (VCO₂), while the pulse oximeter measures peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO₂) and pulse rate.

Together, these measurements can help assess responses to physical activity, estimate energy expenditure, and evaluate aerobic capacity when appropriate testing protocols are used.

This information is valuable for understanding how astronauts adapt physically and metabolically to prolonged periods in space.

3. Muscle health and physical deconditioning

Muscle loss is another important concern during space missions. Without the usual mechanical loading caused by Earth's gravity, muscles can gradually lose mass and function.

To support muscle monitoring, HANAN PACHA proposes the use of portable ultrasound to evaluate characteristics such as muscle thickness and architecture.

By comparing measurements taken at different stages of a mission, astronauts and medical teams could better understand how muscle structure changes over time and assess the effects of exercise programs and other preventive measures.

4. Radiation exposure monitoring

Radiation is a major concern for astronauts, particularly during missions beyond Earth's protective magnetic field.

HANAN PACHA includes the proposed integration of a personal dosimeter to record radiation exposure and track cumulative dose throughout a mission, according to the measurements supported by the device.

Having this information in one place would make it easier to follow individual exposure over time and provide useful records for radiation surveillance and risk assessment.

5. Cognitive performance and attention assessment

Astronauts need to remain alert and make accurate decisions, even when dealing with fatigue, demanding workloads, and disrupted sleep schedules.

For this reason, HANAN PACHA incorporates the three-minute Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT-B), which evaluates sustained attention and reaction time, including delayed responses and lapses in vigilance.

Repeating this assessment throughout a mission can help identify changes in individual cognitive performance and indicate when further evaluation may be necessary.

6. Sleep and psychological well-being

Physical health is only one part of astronaut well-being. Living and working in an isolated and confined environment can also affect sleep, mood, and psychological adaptation.

HANAN PACHA includes a digital module for regular sleep and mental health assessments. One of the proposed tools is the 23-item Mental Health Checklist (MHCL), which allows psychological responses to be recorded and followed over time.

These assessments can help document changes in well-being and provide additional context when reviewing an astronaut's overall health.

They are especially relevant during long missions, when separation from family, limited personal space, demanding routines, and changes in sleep patterns may influence mental health and performance.

7. Integrated health information and medical decision support

Perhaps the most important benefit of HANAN PACHA is that it connects information that would otherwise be reviewed separately.

Cardiovascular, respiratory, metabolic, muscular, radiation-related, cognitive, and psychological measurements can be organised into an individual health record that evolves throughout the mission.

This makes it easier to compare results over time, explore possible relationships between different health indicators, and recognize changes that may require medical attention.

The platform is also designed to accommodate additional devices and assessment tools as the project develops.

Ultimately, we want HANAN PACHA to make astronaut health monitoring more connected, understandable, and useful. Rather than replacing medical professionals, our goal is to provide organized information that supports their assessments while helping astronauts take a more active role in understanding their own health.

As space missions become longer and take humans farther from Earth, we believe this kind of integrated monitoring could make a meaningful contribution to astronaut safety, medical autonomy, and research into human adaptation to space.

3. What is the anticipated impact of the project?

Long-duration space missions expose the human body to conditions that can compromise multiple physiological systems. Microgravity promotes cardiovascular adaptations, muscle loss, and metabolic alterations, while isolation, sleep disturbances, and ionizing radiation may affect cognitive performance and psychological well-being.

To address these challenges, HANAN PACHA proposes a multidimensional health monitoring platform that integrates biomedical information to support the longitudinal assessment of astronaut health. Its anticipated impact encompasses three dimensions:

- Biomedical and Scientific Impact:Facilitating the study of physiological adaptations to space through the integration of cardiovascular, respiratory, metabolic, muscular, radiation-related, and neuropsychological indicators, contributing to research in space physiology and countermeasure assessment.

-Operational Impact:Centralizing relevant health information to identify changes in health indicators, support preventive surveillance, and inform medical decision-making, particularly during missions where communication with Earth and access to healthcare resources are limited.

- Terrestrial Impact:*Extending its potential applications to isolated and extreme environments, including Antarctic stations, space analog habitats, scientific expeditions, and remote communities, where comprehensive health monitoring remains challenging.

In the long term, HANAN PACHA aims to contribute to a more integrated, preventive, and human-centered approach to aerospace medicine, supporting astronaut safety and medical autonomy

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project? 

We built HANAN PACHA using a JAMstack/SPA + Serverless architecture with React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3, JSON, and Vite.

For 3D visualization, we used Three.js and React Three Fiber so users can interactively view the anatomical model and biomedical devices from multiple angles, while Apache ECharts and Chart.js display health indicators and trends.

We integrated an AI voice assistant powered by Google Gemini, Groq, and speech recognition/generation technologies so users can ask health questions. Local data is stored via IndexedDB, and the app is developed and deployed using GitHub and Vercel.

Currently, the prototype relies on virtual 3D devices and synthetic health data rather than physical medical equipment.

How is your project creative?

What makes HANAN PACHA different is the way we bring together astronaut health monitoring, interactive technology, and personalized information in a single platform.

We wanted to go beyond traditional dashboards that display medical measurements as numbers and graphs. Instead, we developed an interactive 3D anatomical model that allows astronauts to explore different areas of the body and understand which health indicators may need attention.

Another important feature is our personalized monitoring approach. Rather than relying only on general reference values, HANAN PACHA compares measurements with each astronaut's own 14-day baseline. This helps highlight changes that may be relevant to their individual health.

We also integrated cognitive and psychological assessments, radiation exposure tracking, health trends, and an AI assistant that helps users understand their information and access relevant guidance.

Our project's name is also meaningful to us. HANAN PACHA comes from Quechua and refers to the world above. Through this name, we wanted to connect our Andean cultural heritage with the future of space exploration.

What factors did your team consider?

While developing HANAN PACHA, we focused on the real challenges astronauts may face during long-duration missions, particularly microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, confinement, fatigue, and changes in sleep patterns.

We also considered the difficulties of providing medical assistance when astronauts are far from Earth. Communication delays can make immediate support impossible, so we designed the platform to help crew members understand their health information and recognize when professional medical attention may be needed.

Another important consideration was accessibility. We wanted the information to be clear, visual, and easy to navigate, even for users who may not have extensive medical training.

Data privacy and offline functionality were also part of our design decisions. Since real astronaut medical records are not publicly available, our prototype uses clearly identified synthetic data.

We consulted NASA resources, including NASA-STD-3001 and the Human Research Program, to guide our approach to health monitoring.

Above all, we wanted to create a tool that supports astronauts and medical teams without replacing professional medical judgment. HANAN PACHA is a prototype for health monitoring and decision support, not a medical diagnostic device.
